title: Immediate image generalization of a missing closed boundary point
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $Y$ be an affine scheme locally of finite type over $k$, let $X$ be a scheme locally of finite type over $k$, and let $f:X\to Y$ be a quasi-compact $k$-morphism [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Let $Z\subseteq |X|$ be any closed subset. If $f(Z)$ is not closed in $|Y|$, there exist points $y,t\in Y$ and $x\in Z$ such that $y$ is closed in $Y$, $y\in\overline{f(Z)}\setminus f(Z)$, $f(x)=t$, and $t\ne y$ specializes to $y$ with no intervening point. The extension $\kappa(x)/\kappa(t)$ is finite [def-weil-residue-field]. With its reduced induced closed subscheme structure [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme], $T=\overline{\{t\}}\subseteq Y$ is an integral affine scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-pc-integral-scheme], has generic point $t$, contains $y$ as a closed point, and satisfies $\dim\mathcal O_{T,y}=1$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. The canonical map $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$ [def-pc-scheme-fibre] has image $x$ and its composite with $f$ is the canonical map through $t\in T\subseteq Y$.

source.place: Tag 0GWV, limits-lemma-essentially-finite-type-criterion-universally-closed, proof, paragraph beginning Assume S and Y affine, and the definition of T in the following paragraph; specialize to S=Spec k. The closed-boundary-point choice uses constructibility and the Jacobson property as in the same proof.

proof.text: Write $Y=\operatorname{Spec}R$. By [lem-weil-pbc-lft-affine-pairs], $R$ is a finite type $k$-algebra. For every affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ in $X$, that same criterion makes $B$ a finite type $k$-algebra, hence a finite type $R$-algebra through $f$: any finite set generating $B$ over $k$ also generates it over $R$, because $f$ is a $k$-morphism. The criterion therefore makes $f$ locally of finite type. With its assumed quasi-compactness, $f$ is finite type. Since $Y$ is affine and $f$ is quasi-compact, $X$ is quasi-compact; thus $X$ and $Y$ are finite type over $k$. A field is Noetherian (its only ideals are zero and the whole field), so [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] makes both schemes Noetherian. In particular $Y$ is locally Noetherian. Apply [pqf-lem-lft-fp-locnoeth] to make $f$ locally of finite presentation.

source.place: Tags 01T2 (lemma-locally-finite-type-characterize), 01T6 (lemma-finite-type-noetherian); Tag 01TX for finite presentation over a locally Noetherian base.

proof.text: The affine charts of $X$ have Noetherian coordinate rings by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian], applied to their finite type $k$-algebras from step 1. Their topological spaces are Noetherian by [lem-sc-affine-noetherian-underlying-space]. A finite such cover exists since $X$ is quasi-compact; a descending chain of closed subsets stabilizes on each chart, hence on $X$. Thus $Z$ is constructible by [def-weil-constructible-subset]. The target $Y$ is affine, hence quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-chevalley-constructible-image] to $f$ and $Z$ to see that $E=f(Z)$ is constructible.

The nonclosedness of $E$ says that $D=\overline E\setminus E$ is nonempty. It is constructible by the Boolean-algebra and Noetherian clauses of [def-weil-constructible-subset]; $Y$ is topologically Noetherian by the same affine argument as step 2. Express $D$ as a finite union of locally closed sets and choose a nonempty piece $W=O\cap F$, where $O$ is open and $F$ is closed in $Y$. By [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space], the closed points of $Y$ lying in $F$ are dense in $F$. They meet the nonempty relatively open subset $W$ of $F$. Choose such a point $y$. Then $y$ is closed in $Y$ and lies in $\overline E\setminus E$.

source.place: Tag 0GWV (lemma-essentially-finite-type-criterion-universally-closed), paragraph Assume S and Y affine; Morphisms Tag 02J6(1), with the closed-boundary-point choice expanded.

proof.text: The affine scheme $Y$ is spectral by [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-scheme-spectral]. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-spectral-proconstructible-closure-specialization] to the one-member family consisting of $E$ and the point $y\in\overline E$. Obtain $e\in E$ generalizing $y$; it differs from $y$. Put $A=\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ and let $c:\operatorname{Spec}A\to Y$ be [lem-weil-pbc-spec-local-ring-canonical-morphism]. This morphism identifies $A$ with $R_{\mathfrak m_y}$ and its image with the generalizations of $y$. Hence $e$ is in its image. The ring $R$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian], so $A$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-noetherian]. It is a nonzero local ring, since it has the residue field $\kappa(y)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-spectrum-embedding], $c$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, and its closed point maps to $y$.

source.place: Tag 0GWV, intersection with the local spectrum; nonemptiness expanded using Topology Tag 0903(1); Algebra Tags 00FN and 00E3.

proof.text: Let $P=\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus\{\mathfrak m_A\}$. The inverse image $c^{-1}(E)$ is constructible by [lem-pur-scheme-constructible-preimage]; it is nonempty by step 4 and misses $\mathfrak m_A$ since $y\notin E$. Restricting to the open subspace $P$ preserves constructibility by [lem-weil-pbc-constructible-open-restriction]. By [def-weil-constructible-subset], choose a nonempty locally closed piece $W$ of this inverse image in $P$. Apply [lem-sfb-punctured-local-spectrum-closed-points] to the nonzero Noetherian local ring $A$ and $W$. Obtain a point $u\in W$ closed in $P$, and set $t=c(u)\in E$. Every prime of a local ring is contained in its maximal ideal, so $u$ specializes to $\mathfrak m_A$. Closedness of $u$ in $P$ excludes any distinct specialization there. The embedding of step 4 therefore shows that $t\ne y$ specializes to $y$ with no intervening point of $Y$: every intervening point would still generalize $y$, hence lie in that embedding's image.

source.place: Tag 0GWV, choice of t in the punctured local spectrum; Morphisms Tag 02J6(4), Topology Tag 005X.

proof.text: Let $\mathfrak p\subset R$ be the prime of $t$. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-irreducible-closed-subsets-primes], $\overline{\{t\}}=V(\mathfrak p)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme], its reduced induced scheme is $T=\operatorname{Spec}(R/\mathfrak p)$. The quotient is a domain, since $\mathfrak p$ is prime, and is a finite type $k$-algebra, generated by the images of generators of $R$. Thus $T$ is integral, affine, and finite type, with generic point $t$, and $y$ is still closed in $T$. Its generalizations of $y$ are precisely $y$ and $t$. Indeed, a point of $T$ is a specialization of $t$; any such point generalizing $y$ would intervene between $t$ and $y$. Hence the generalization chains starting at $y$ have maximum length one. Apply [lem-sc-scheme-stalk-dimension-generalization-chains] to $T,y$ to obtain $\dim\mathcal O_{T,y}=1$.

source.place: Tag 0GWV, paragraph defining T; Schemes Tags 01J3--01J4; Properties Tag 02IZ (lemma-codimension-local-ring).

proof.text: Give $Z$ its reduced induced closed subscheme structure by [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme]. Its affine charts are quotients of the affine charts of $X$, hence finite type over $k$ and, by the same generator argument as step 1, over $Y$. Thus $g:Z\to Y$ is locally of finite type by [lem-weil-pbc-lft-affine-pairs]. Since $t\in f(Z)$, its fibre $Z_t$ is nonempty by [def-pc-scheme-fibre]. It is locally of finite type over $K=\kappa(t)$ by [lem-weil-pbc-lft-base-change]. Choose a nonempty affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ in $Z_t$. Then $B$ is a finite type $K$-algebra by the affine-pairs criterion. Choose a maximal ideal of this nonzero ring by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal], giving a closed point $v\in V$. Apply [lem-kun-closed-point-field](a) to the finite type $K$-scheme $V$: its residue field is finite over $K$.

source.place: Tag 01TF (lemma-closed-point-fibre-locally-finite-type), proof by an affine chart and the Hilbert Nullstellensatz; as used in Tag 0GWV.

proof.text: Let $z\in Z$ be the image of $v$ and $x\in X$ its image. Thus $x\in Z$ and $f(x)=t$. The open immersion $V\hookrightarrow Z_t$ induces an isomorphism on residue fields by [lem-weil-pbc-residue-field-point-naturality]. The fibre stalk quotient of [lem-sbc-scheme-fibre-stalk-quotient] identifies $\mathcal O_{Z_t,v}$ with $\mathcal O_{Z,z}/\mathfrak m_t\mathcal O_{Z,z}$. Passing to residue fields gives $\kappa(v)=\kappa(z)$: the ideal being divided out lies in the maximal ideal, and quotienting once more by that maximal ideal is the original residue field. These are identifications over $K$, since the quotient is induced by the fibre projection and structure map. The closed immersion $Z\hookrightarrow X$ induces $\kappa(x)\cong\kappa(z)$ by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-residue-field-iso]. Consequently $\kappa(x)/\kappa(t)$ is finite. Finally [def-pc-scheme-fibre] gives the canonical point map $j_x:\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X$ with image $x$. Naturality [lem-weil-pbc-residue-field-point-naturality] gives $fj_x=j_t\operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(t)\to\kappa(x))$. Applying the same naturality to $T\hookrightarrow Y$ at its generic point $t$, and using the residue-field isomorphism for that closed immersion, identifies $j_t$ with its canonical factorization through $T$. This is the required compatibility.
